solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Member turned, with no flaws, to do preparatory exercise

indicators.note: A word turned round is read backwards.

blocks.note: an arm or leg is a member of the body
with no flaws = PURE, turned to read backwards

explanation.surface: A gymnast twists a limb and, finding nothing wrong, starts warming up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' sits beside 'Member' and looks as if it acts on it, but it works on the phrase after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To limber up is to loosen the body with light exercise before exertion.

clue.text: Coming up at regular intervals, Diane’s rent

indicators.note: Take every other letter, here the second, fourth and sixth of DIANES.

blocks.note: rent = tore, the past tense of rend

explanation.surface: A notice that Diane's rent falls due every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' reads as money owed; it is the past tense of rend, TORE. 'Coming up' looks like a reversal sign in a down clue but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: What is in store for you is coming up, waiting ahead.

clue.text: Tame reindeer is one performing to music

blocks.note: to break a horse is to tame it
Dancer is one of Santa's reindeer

explanation.surface: A domesticated reindeer turns out to be a circus act that performs to music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tame reindeer' reads as adjective and noun; in fact 'Tame' is a verb, BREAK, and the reindeer is named: Dancer, from the Christmas poem.
explanation.definitionFit: A breakdancer performs acrobatic street dance to music.

clue.text: Fluid from pen numpty emptied

indicators.note: An emptied word loses all its inside letters, keeping only the first and last.

blocks.note: a run is an enclosure for animals, as in a chicken run

explanation.surface: Ink leaks from the pen of some fool who has emptied it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' suggests writing and ink; it is the animal enclosure. A numpty is a Scottish slang word for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Something runny is fluid, flowing like liquid.

clue.text: Make brownish-pink shade to shelter staff

indicators.note: One word shelters another by going round it.

blocks.note: a rod is a staff or stick

explanation.surface: A decorator mixes a pinkish-brown paint to protect the staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees; it is a stick, and the colour name wraps round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to produce goods or a result is to bring it into being.

clue.text: Discarded material by far side of the grate

indicators.note: The far side of a word is its last letter.

explanation.surface: Rubbish piled up beside a fireplace grate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grate' looks like the fireplace noun; it is the verb, to scrape.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb sense: grating cheese, or a nail down a board, means rubbing it against a rough edge.

clue.text: City guard circling base very loudly

indicators.note: One word circles another by going round it.

blocks.note: e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A sentry patrols a military base, shouting as he goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' is a mathematical one: e, the base of natural logarithms, not a military camp.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this Yorkshire steel town is one of England's large cities.

clue.text: Uncooked crustacean shelled

indicators.note: Shelling a word strips its outer letters, first and last.

blocks.note: PRAWN without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A peeled prawn that has not been cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is literal kitchen talk: a shelled, uncooked prawn. The word 'shelled' does the same job on the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: meat or vegetables not yet cooked are described as raw.

clue.text: Transaction type organised with man

indicators.note: Letters organised are rearranged into a new order.

explanation.surface: A kind of deal set up with some man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transaction type' reads as a single phrase, but the definition stops at 'Transaction'; 'type' belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: handing over money is the commonest kind of transaction.

clue.text: Being willing to get in repaired swing

blocks.note: to get a point is to see it
to repair to a place is to go there

explanation.surface: Someone happily gets back into a mended garden swing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repaired' reads as mended; it is the old sense 'went', as in 'repaired to the bar'. 'Seeing one's way to' doing something means being willing to do it.
explanation.definitionFit: If you can see your way to doing something, you are willing to do it.

clue.text: Sport clubs mock hosts

indicators.note: A word hosts another by taking it inside.

explanation.surface: A sports club that plays host to fake events.
explanation.walkthrough: Hockey is played with clubs, so 'clubs' seems to belong with 'Sport'; it is only C. 'Clubs' pulling double duty tempts JOCKEY, but there is no J.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: hockey, played with sticks and a ball, is one of many sports.

clue.text: Very enjoyable taking out first female available

indicators.note: Remove the first of the named letter.

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation, removed from the front

explanation.surface: A single woman described as great fun and on the market.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first F goes; the second, in FILLED, stays. An unfilled post is one still available.
explanation.definitionFit: An unfilled vacancy or seat is available to take.

clue.text: Playing on console, an unpredictable person

indicators.note: Letters playing move about into a new order.

explanation.surface: A gamer at the console who behaves erratically.
explanation.walkthrough: The article 'an' reads as part of the definition but is fodder; the definition is only 'unpredictable person'.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose cannon is someone whose unpredictable behaviour may cause damage.

clue.text: Sportsperson cut man with hard jabs

indicators.note: Something that jabs pokes into, so goes inside.

blocks.note: cat is slang for a man, a guy

explanation.surface: A boxer takes a cut from an opponent who jabs hard.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxing picture points to a fighter; 'jabs' is only an insertion sign. CAT, jazz slang for a man, plus H go into DE…LETE.
explanation.definitionFit: A decathlete competes in the ten-event decathlon.

clue.text: Blend is used in injury unit

indicators.note: IS is put to use inside the following word.

explanation.surface: A mixture of ingredients applied in a hospital's injury unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Injury unit' reads as a hospital ward; the two words split and IS goes into the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To harmonise is to blend parts together agreeably.

clue.text: Suspicious of donations at prime locations

indicators.note: Number the letters and keep those at prime-numbered positions: 2, 3, 5 and 7.

explanation.surface: A charity grows wary of gifts turning up at suspiciously good addresses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime locations' is estate-agent talk for the best spots; here it means the prime-numbered letter positions.
explanation.definitionFit: If you are onto someone, you suspect what they are up to.

clue.text: Love habitual twitching of the ear

blocks.note: love = nil = O, from tennis scoring
a tic is a habitual twitch

explanation.surface: A lover's ear that keeps twitching.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs 'twitching of the ear' together, but 'of the ear' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A technical adjective built on the Greek word for ear, as in otitis.

clue.text: Raised money with pub band seen on screen

indicators.note: In a down clue, raising a word writes it upwards, so it reads backwards.

blocks.note: money = LOOT, slang; raised, so written upwards

explanation.surface: A pub band raises money and ends up on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised money' reads as fundraising; 'Raised' is the reversal sign and 'band' belongs to the definition, a strip on a computer screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A toolbar is the strip of buttons across the top of a computer window.

clue.text: Parliamentary supporters harass Communists according to Spooner

indicators.note: Swap the opening sounds of the two words, as Rev. Spooner reputedly did.

blocks.note: to hound is to harass; it takes the R from the second word
reds = Communists; it takes the H from the first word

explanation.surface: Politicians' backers set about hounding the Communists.
explanation.walkthrough: Roundheads were the supporters of Parliament against the King in the English Civil War, so 'Parliamentary' means that side, not today's MPs.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roundheads backed Parliament in the English Civil War, named for their cropped hair.

clue.text: Prudent being prepared for economic growth?

indicators.note: Letters being prepared are worked into a new form.

explanation.surface: A cautious economist gets ready for a boom.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that an uptrend is only one kind of economic growth, an example rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: An uptrend is an upward movement, as in an economy or market.

clue.text: Fault of French motor initially with exhaust upside-down

indicators.note: Initially means at the start, so only the word's opening letter is used.
In a down clue, a word upside-down reads bottom to top, so backwards.

explanation.surface: A mechanic reports a fault in a French car: the exhaust is fitted upside-down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhaust' reads as a car part in this garage scene; it is the verb, TIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A demerit is a fault or a black mark against someone.

clue.text: Upright member is good sport missing golf shot

indicators.note: The named letter goes missing.
Something shot is ruined, its letters scrambled.

blocks.note: G in the NATO alphabet, dropped

explanation.surface: A decent club member graciously misses a golf shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright member' sounds like a respectable club member; it is a vertical timber. 'Shot' reads as a golf stroke but is the anagram sign.
explanation.definitionFit: The carpentry sense of member: a structural piece, here the vertical timber at the side of a door frame.

clue.text: Conservative and Labour front-bencher close

blocks.note: David Lammy, a senior Labour politician

explanation.surface: A Tory and a Labour frontbencher are on close terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close' reads as friendly, but it is weather: humid and sticky. David Lammy is a leading British Labour politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Close weather is humid and oppressive, the kind that leaves skin clammy.

clue.text: Confusion over plugging bottomless pit

indicators.note: A word plugging another fills a gap inside it.
In a down clue the bottom is the last letter, which goes.

blocks.note: a chasm is a deep pit

explanation.surface: Workers are baffled trying to fill a pit with no bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottomless pit' reads as one phrase; 'bottomless' only trims CHASM before O goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: complete disorder, where nobody knows what is going on.

clue.text: Doctor’s practice by nobleman’s estate reportedly housing duke

indicators.note: A word housing another holds it inside.
Reported speech: the word as said, not as spelt.

blocks.note: a manor is a lord's estate

explanation.surface: A GP's surgery sits beside a lord's country estate, where a duke is staying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Practice' looks like a doctor's surgery building; it is how a doctor behaves with patients.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedside manner is the way a doctor behaves towards patients.

clue.text: Exhausted, stopped working with energy lacking

indicators.note: The named letter is taken out.

blocks.note: a machine that died stopped working

explanation.surface: A worn-out worker downs tools, completely out of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Think of 'did' as in 'we did the museum', covering it all: to exhaust a subject is to do it completely.
explanation.definitionFit: To do a place or topic thoroughly is to exhaust it, so did = exhausted.

clue.text: Game where Jack has commanding position

blocks.note: Jack = a sailor (Jack Tar); the commanding position is the ship's command post

explanation.surface: A card game in which the jack outranks the other cards.
explanation.walkthrough: In a card game Jack looks like the playing card; here Jack is a sailor (Jack Tar), and the bridge is where a ship is commanded.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridge is a card game, and a ship's bridge is its command post.

clue.text: Separate from group in market in US idly going round

indicators.note: The answer lies inside the words that follow.
Turned round, so read backwards.

blocks.clueFragment: market in US idly going round
blocks.note: marK(ET IN US ID)ly holds the letters, read backwards

explanation.surface: A US market drifting aimlessly, apart from the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The run lies across three words and reads backwards, from the D of 'idly' to the E of 'market'.
explanation.definitionFit: To disunite is to split apart what was united.
